content: Human hair color is determined by the pigmentation of hair follicles, which is influenced by two types of melanin: eumelanin and pheomelanin. The amount and type of melanin present dictate the darkness or lightness of the hair. Higher melanin levels result in darker hair, while lower levels produce lighter hair. Over time, hair color can change due to fluctuations in melanin production, and individuals may have hair follicles of varying colors. Global migration and travel have contributed to significant diversity in hair color, even among individuals of similar ethnic backgrounds. Genetics and Biochemistry of Hair Color Hair color is primarily determined by two pigments: eumelanin and pheomelanin. Pheomelanin is responsible for red hair, while eumelanin, which exists in black and brown subtypes, determines the darkness of hair. Low concentrations of brown eumelanin result in blonde hair, while higher concentrations produce brown hair. Black eumelanin in high amounts leads to black hair, whereas low levels of black eumelanin result in gray hair. All humans have varying amounts of pheomelanin, though it is most noticeable in red-haired individuals. Pheomelanin is chemically more stable than black eumelanin but less stable than brown eumelanin, which explains why darker hair turns reddish-brown during bleaching. As pheomelanin continues to degrade, the hair transitions through orange, yellow, and eventually white. The genetics of hair color are complex and not fully understood. One theory suggests that at least two gene pairs control hair color. One gene pair involves a dominant brown allele and a recessive blonde allele, where the presence of a brown allele results in brown hair, and the absence of brown alleles results in blonde hair. This explains how two brown-haired parents can have a blonde-haired child. The second gene pair involves a dominant not-red allele and a recessive red allele. Individuals with two copies of the red allele will have red hair, but the shade (auburn or bright reddish-orange) depends on the first gene pair's influence. However, this two-gene model does not account for all hair color variations, such as platinum blonde or dark blonde, nor does it explain why hair often darkens with age. Multiple gene pairs likely contribute cumulatively to the lightness or darkness of hair color, and environmental factors can interact with genetic predispositions to produce diverse phenotypes. Natural Hair Colors Natural hair colors include black, brown, blonde, red, gray, and white, with variations influenced by genetic and ethnic factors. Hair color is often associated with specific skin tones and eye colors. Black Hair Black hair is the darkest and most common hair color globally. It contains high levels of eumelanin and is less dense than other hair colors. Brown Hair Brown hair is the second most common hair color and is prevalent in Europe. It is characterized by high levels of dark eumelanin and lower levels of pale pheomelanin. Brown-haired individuals typically have medium-thick hair strands and are often referred to as brunettes. Blonde Hair Blonde hair ranges from nearly white (platinum blonde) to dark golden blonde. Strawberry blonde, a mix of blonde and red hair, is rare and contains the highest amounts of pheomelanin. Blonde hair typically has small amounts of both pheomelanin and eumelanin. Higher pheomelanin levels result in golden blonde shades, while higher eumelanin levels produce ash blonde. Blonde hair is common in European populations but rare in non-European groups. Many children born with blonde hair develop darker hair as they age. Auburn Hair Auburn hair varies from light to reddish-brown and is caused by a combination of brown eumelanin and pheomelanin. It is most commonly found in individuals of European descent. Red Hair Red hair, the rarest distinct hair color, ranges from vivid strawberry shades to deep auburn and burgundy. It is caused by a variation in the MC1R gene and is believed to be recessive. Red hair has the highest levels of pheomelanin and usually low levels of eumelanin. Gray and White Hair Gray hair typically appears as people age due to a reduction in melanin production. In some cases, gray or white hair can occur at a young age due to genetic factors, thyroid deficiencies, or vitamin B12 deficiency. The cessation of melanin production in hair roots leads to the growth of unpigmented hair. The death of melanocyte stem cells at the base of hair follicles is responsible for the onset of graying. Conditions Affecting Hair Color Effects of Aging on Hair Color Hair color often darkens during childhood and adolescence. Over time, hair naturally turns gray and eventually white as melanin production ceases. Genetics largely determine the age at which graying begins. Some individuals are born with gray hair due to inherited traits. Two genes, Bcl2 and Bcl-w, are thought to regulate the graying process. The death of melanocyte stem cells halts melanin production, leading to gray or white hair. Other Medical Conditions Albinism is a genetic condition characterized by little or no pigment in the hair, skin, and eyes, resulting in pale skin, white or pale blonde hair, and gray, blue, or purple eyes. Vitiligo, an autoimmune condition, causes patchy loss of hair and skin color. Malnutrition can lead to lighter, thinner, and more brittle hair due to decreased melanin production, which is reversible with proper nutrition. Werner syndrome and pernicious anemia can also cause premature graying. Smoking has been linked to premature graying, with smokers being four times more likely to gray early compared to non-smokers. Temporary darkening of gray hair can occur after inflammatory processes, electron-beam-induced alopecia, or certain chemotherapy regimens. Changes in Hair Color After Death The hair color of mummies or buried bodies can change over time due to the breakdown of pigments. Eumelanin, being less chemically stable than pheomelanin, degrades faster when oxidized, which explains why Egyptian mummies often have reddish hair. Hair color changes more rapidly under extreme conditions and more slowly in dry, oxidizing environments (e.g., sand or ice burials) compared to wet, reducing conditions (e.g., wood or plaster coffins). Hair Coloring Hair color can be altered through chemical processes, either permanently or temporarily. Permanent hair coloring involves the removal of natural pigment, which does not return. Semi-permanent hair color can darken or change tonal values but cannot lighten hair and typically washes out after several shampoos. Temporary hair color, such as rinses, lasts only until the next wash. Permanent hair color is widely used but requires frequent reapplication and may result in issues like fading or uneven color.
